utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case Number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecution versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good afternoon. The Trial Chamber is pleased to continue the proceedings today. We have been joined by Judge Lindholm, who was appointed by the Secretary-General to continue with the trial in this case. I see that we have a witness already. Can the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, and welcome, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you state your name, please.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Nusret Hadzijusufovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when were you born, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of October, 1947, in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: A son and a daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Any grandchildren?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I have two granddaughters and one grandson.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long has your family lived in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: My family is one of the first families who settled in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did your father live there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Grandfather?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Great-grandfather?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you have any close family members, close family members, still living there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I have two relatives on my father's side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what about the rest of your relatives? Why aren't they living there any more?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: They were all expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let us go to your educational background. Where did you attend primary school?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: In Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you attend secondary school?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: In Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you study there, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I finished schooling for a -- training for a lathe operator. It was a school for vocational training.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And after graduation, what did you do for work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I worked as a lathe operator in the Mebos factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where was the Mebos factory located, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The Mebos factory was located on Edvard Kardelja Street in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did they do at that company, what sort of work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It was a factory producing water heaters and construction trolleys, barrels, and such like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And during what years did you work there on a full-time basis?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: From 1966 until the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever serve in the military, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I did my military service in 1967, 1968 in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, are you a member of any ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do you practice any religion?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the League of Communists for 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: After you completed that 20-year period with the League of Communists, did you join any other parties?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I joined the SDP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is that the Social Democrat party?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how long were you a member of that party?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Until the war, for four or five years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was your name ever on the ballot? Was it ever placed on the ballot by the SDP party, meaning the Social Democrat party?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In what year?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Just before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was that 1991 or 1992, if you recall, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It was at the elections just before the war, in 1992. Sorry, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how did your party do in the election?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Poorly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the SDA party in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the president of that party was?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Sulejman Tihic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of that party?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the president of that party was in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the HDZ party?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of that party?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do you know who the president of that party was in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Mato Nujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever own a firearm?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: A hunting rifle of any kind?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about a home? Did you own a home in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where was your home located?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: On Vuk Karadzic Street, number 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And who lived with you at your home?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Myself, my wife, and our two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you have any business also located on that property?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: For six months, six months before the war, my wife became unemployed, and we opened a kabob kiosk.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Chamber what exactly a kabob kiosk is, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It's a small shop, a small business, that made food, kabobs catering to the citizenry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, having lived your whole life in Bosanski Samac, I'm going to ask you if you know some people. Do you know a man named Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many years or how long have you known Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I've known him for 30 years, since primary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you, sir, to look around the courtroom, and can you tell me if you see Simo Zaric in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It's the man sitting next to the policeman. He's wearing glasses, grey hair, and his -- he looks the same as before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What colour is his suit, if you can tell?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Black. That man over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man by the name of Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It's the one with the grey moustache. He looks the same as before the war. He's just a little stouter. The one over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man by the name of Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I know him as a doctor. It's the one with the goatee. He didn't have it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And is he sitting in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I see him. It's the one in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the record reflect that all three defendants have been identified by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with a military unit known as the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what exactly was it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It was a paramilitary unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether it was tied to any political party?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It was, to the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what's the basis of that opinion, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I saw before the war and during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know who organised that unit?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who organised the unit?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Those people sitting here, the people I mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you referring to the defendants?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether that military unit ever held trainings?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: They did. They held drills near the Bosna River in a place called Sokolusa. They usually set off to those drills from the AS Cafe, and some arrived straight from their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: During what month, if you recall, what month and year, did these drills, these military drills, take place?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It was perhaps a month or two before the war. Until the outbreak of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So are we talking about from February on, or March on, of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that on occasion, some of the soldiers came from or would gather and come from the Cafe AS. Do you know who owned the Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever view any of these trainings or drills?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: On a couple of occasions, two or three times, perhaps. Once, I watched from the weekend cottage belonging to the Petic family, once from the embankment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: During any of these trainings, were any of the defendants present?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: On one occasion, I saw Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know who trained these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: They were trained by Mladen Roda.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether JNA instructors were used during these trainings?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: They were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How do you know that that they weren't JNA soldiers that were serving as instructors?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I know because I knew the people who were training those men who were moving around. I could see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The people who were being trained from the 4th Detachment, how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: They were all wearing civilian clothes at the outset, and it was only at a later stage that they started wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the members of the 4th Detachment were being paid prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I know they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I know because individuals told us around town at the time when enterprises began to fall apart and many people were left unemployed, some of them joined this paramilitary unit in Samac. And after that, individuals would walk around town carrying large amounts of cash. Some of them addressed me personally, including Tota and Ibrahim Fleka. They would say, "Go to Miro and take the money and join us, rather than walk around town, penniless."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man by the name of Mujo Omeranovic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I know him. I know her. It's Simo Zaric's sister, married to Mujaga, Mujo Omeranovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know where this person lived?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: He's a neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let us move to the late evening of April 1st, 1992. Did you see Mujo, if I am pronouncing the name right, your neighbour, on the street with some trucks?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I was coming back home between 10.00 and half past 10.00 from visiting my parents, and on the corner of Vuk Karadzic Street and the Djura Zelkovic [phoen] Street, I saw two trucks, but I was used to seeing some trucks on our street with the drivers. But just after making the turn, I noticed some vehicles outside Rirko's [phoen] house, or rather Stanko's house. I quickened my step, and I noticed that those two trucks -- I noticed those two trucks, and Simo Zaric and Mujuga standing in front of my mother's house, and they were unloading something from the trucks. And I saw another two men standing just beside the truck. I walked towards them hurriedly, and I saw them carrying a case with weapons. Mujo and Simo Zaric were standing right next to Mujo's mother's house. That's the same courtyard. I hurried home, and I told my wife about what I had seen. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: These cases, can you describe the size of these cases that they were carrying?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It was one case carried by two men, and the other cases were on the truck. It was a case about a metre in length, military-type case, rectangular, with two handles made of cord on each side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen cases like that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what are they used for, those types of cases?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: They are used for storing weapons. There was a smaller type of case used usually for Kalashnikov-type rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where were they bringing these cases, as best you could tell?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: They were carrying them towards Mujo's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know a man by the name of Slobodan Kukrika?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I know him. Four or five days after this thing I mentioned seeing, my next-door neighbour invited me to his house and showed me the rifle that he had got. And he told me, "Look, look at this rifle. I got it from Mujo." I looked at the rifle. It wasn't a rifle of the size that could fit into that case. It was longer. He told me it was a 4, a submachine-gun actually, and he described it to me in detail. Later on, I learned from a couple of my friends including Came, that they, too, had got weapons. I knew about it. Later, when I dug trenches along the fence lines, I heard stories from other men. Because all the weaponry that was issued in Samac was issued out of houses, out of private houses, because at the headquarters of the Territorial Defence, the premises were occupied by a camp, and the headquarters had been moved out. All the weapons had been moved out. I know that building, the headquarters, because I went there for drills, and I entered the storage room on occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's just go back a little bit. You said you knew Slobodan Kukrika, who got the gun. Where does he live in relation to you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Next door to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So when you say your next-door neighbour got a gun from Mujo, are you talking about Slobodan Kukrika?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that was five days after you saw those boxes being delivered to Muja's house?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether Mr. Kukrika was a member of any military unit in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was a member of the 4th detachment?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was he a soldier?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the 4th detachment during the war, but I don't know about before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, so this Mr. Kukrika who received the Kalishnikov was a member of the 4th detachment during the war; you mean in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: From the first day onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, these other persons who told you that they received weapons, do you know what, if any, military unit they belonged to during the war, in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: They were all belonged to the 4th detachment. While prior to the war, they didn't participate. I only knew who was standing in front of Cafe AS, who were those who went and attended the military training as I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: On what street was Miroslav Tadic's Cafe AS located in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: In the Edvard Kardelja Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where was that located in relation to your home and your place of work at the Mebos company?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That was in the same street as the factory company Mebos. And as far as my home is concerned, it was some 300, 400 metres from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how did you get to work each day, to the Mebos company, from your home?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I went from my home passing the hospital, Cafe AS. There's a crossroads before the Cafe AS, and then straight to Mebos company. From 1966 to the beginning of the war, the same direction, the same movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you said you passed it, did you walk each day, or did you drive passed these places?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have a car. I usually walked, and occasionally I used a bicycle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever patronise the Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, occasionally, when I ended my second shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When was that, what time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That was approximately from 8.00 to 10.00 p.m., around 10.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let us go to the first week of April of 1992. And did you notice anything as you walked past the Cafe AS, as you went to and from work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That cafe, prior to the war, had a good turnover, always packed with patrons, always full of people whom I saw later in the 4th detachment, who were commanders of the 4th detachment later. 90 per cent or 99 per cent of them were members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with the SIT company?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: SIT company is located on the other side of the road of the cafe, and immediately after the outbreak of the war, everybody moved to the SIT company, members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What sort of work was done at the SIT company, if you know, prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Also my wife worked at producing knitwear, sweaters, T-shirts. It was a textile industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How was it used after the war started?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It was used for military purposes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It was used by the very same people who were in the 4th Detachment, the people who congregated in the AS cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How, what happened to all the equipment that had been in that company, in that cafe -- I'm sorry, in the SIT company?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The equipment was moved to the neighbouring factory, Tekstilac, which produced apparel. But they didn't have similar type of production, so everything was moved from this factory to the factory Tekstilac, very close by in the same street of Edvard Kardelja.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know who moved the equipment from the SIT company?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: We moved it. We, who were mobilised to do forced labour. I didn't participate in that, but while working in Tekstilac, I saw Marijan Toravic [phoen], a man with a bypass, the director for economic issues. And he was forced to work in the moving of this equipment. He was in forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say a man with a bypass, can you explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that such a person with -- so sick, he was forced to do such heavy labour, physical labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say he had a bypass, do you mean a heart bypass surgery? Is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know a man by the name of Nizam Ramusovic, nicknamed Tota?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, quite well. That was a labourer who worked in the municipal company. And he was among the first of the 4th Detachment -- members of the 4th Detachment. He was also visited Cafe AS. He was a person who was a loafer, and a person who for money switched and joined the 4th Detachment. He was from Samac. I knew him quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was he an intelligent man?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours, calling for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The witness did say he knew him?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, but Your Honours, the category of intelligence is something which is rather very broad. So maybe even an expert can be in a hard position to give the opinion of someone, whether he's intelligent or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps Mr. Weiner can ask his witness, if he still insists, by what standards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was involved in a shooting, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour? That was a person who used to fight, a person who abandoned his family completely, a person who excessively drank alcohol, and a person you could name a number of names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, prior to the military take of Bosanski Samac, was Nizam Ramusovic involved in a shooting of some kind?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Nizam Ramusovic, Mirsad Mersad, and a person by the name of Danilo, a few days before the outbreak of war, were in a car and were driving drunk, and they passed through my street three times. They were shooting out of the windows of the car. And throughout the day, they were doing that throughout the town. Then, as dusk, one could hear in my street a lot of weapon fire. I ran out of my house. I could see people gathering. I could see people were congregating in front of Esad's house. I also ran to see what happened. I saw Tota, who was lying wounded on the street near the market. Then I saw Mirsa Mersad, who was also wounded. Danilo was in the neighbouring street at the corner in the car, and nobody, nobody of us present, didn't go and try to help them. Because we all knew these people, everybody knew what they were doing throughout that day. Then a policeman came out, a policeman called Crni, and he used firearms. With a burst of fire, he did that to them. There was Cabasko from the 4th Detachment. Later on, two Lukic's, Nenad and Predo, came. They all came but nobody helped them. My neighbour Sabanovic from the same street had a [unintelligible] automobile, and he then collected them, placed them in the car, and took them to hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a step back. Let me ask you a few questions on this. When you got there, you see two men lying on the street.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And one was Tota and one was Mersad?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mersad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were these men armed with any weapons?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, both of them had Kalishnikovs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And Kalishnikov is an automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, were these persons already injured?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Had these men been shot by the policeman prior to you arriving or did the policeman shoot them after you arrived?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Prior to my arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So they were lying there, and then one of your neighbours, Fadil Sabanovic, took them to a hospital?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Had you ever seen prior to that day Tota and Mersad together?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in front of the Cafe AS. Yes, I did. They were quite prominent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's move to the morning hours of April 17th, the day of the takeover. Can you tell us where you were in those early morning hours, around 2.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I was in my home with my wife and two children. We heard a lot of noise. My wife and I, we went out of the room, went to the attic, and we could see that in the Vuk Karadzic Street, there was nothing. In the other street, we could see two tanks. I took my wife's hand. I said to go down. Then she shouted back, "Come and see." She said, "Soldiers are coming." And I said, "Come down." We could hear a lot of rifle fire from the Ministry of Interior, and other arms fire. I called my wife and then we went downstairs. Then after 10, 15 minutes, we could hear an explosion. Again, we went up to the attic. I moved the tile, roof tile, and I could see the elementary school on fire. We went down to the room, and I said to my wife, "The war has begun. What will we do? What will be with me? What will be with us, with our children? May God help us."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, just one clarification. 17.11, it says, "We could hear a lot of rifle fire from the Ministry of the Interior." I believe the witness had said the police station. But if my learned colleague can clarify this with the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sure, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It was "Mr. Zecevic" in transcript. There's a reference it was me but -- well. Page 17 -- line 17 and 18, just intervention in transcript. You said, "Yes, Mr. Pantelic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Zecevic, and then his answer was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Mr. Zecevic had a question. When you said you could hear rifle fire from the direction of -- did you say the Ministry of the Interior or did you mean the police station, the SUP? Which building could you hear the rifle fire from?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: From the -- from that direction, namely the two buildings are one in proximity of the other, but it was from the direction of the police station. Yes, the police station, SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you make any telephone calls at that time, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: During --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: My wife called her mother in order to ask what is happening there, what was happening? Well, she was rather afraid, so we were all rather afraid. And then my wife invited her to come and stay with us. And that is what she did, in fact. But I did not go.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever see any soldiers during those morning hours?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I saw many soldiers who were moving in my street, one in one direction; the others in the other direction. Of these, I knew many of them, but also quite a few were not from Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you leave the house at any time during those early morning hours?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I did not leave my house. I left -- I went out at 9.00, when two soldiers arrived with insignia of the white eagles. One came up to me and he asked me whether I have weapons. I said no. Then he asked me for my ID. I took it out. He -- I showed it to him, and then they both left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where did this occur?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That happened in my courtyard, in the early morning hours of that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you go beyond your courtyard? Did you go out to the streets during that morning?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No. That day, we did not go out on the street at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, during those first few days after the takeover, did you listen to the radio at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I think the Prosecution should avoid the term "takeover." This notion is under question mark, I think. It's a matter for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So my point, Mr. Weiner can rephrase the issue and take care about that in future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have been using that same term since September of 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pantelic has now reviewed the evidence since the break, and he is putting it on record that it shouldn't be described as a "takeover," for obvious reasons. I think we can stick to "the conflict."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. That was my intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, during those first few days of the conflict, did you and your family listen to the radio?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That our forces, that the Serbian forces liberated Bosanski Samac, and that after a long period of time, the Serbian nation has obtained its freedom. And this was accompanied by battle marches and other patriotic songs and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Patriotic songs of what nationality, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, patriotic and nationalistic songs of the Serbian peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did they say who they liberated the city from?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The city was liberated of the green berets and the Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, prior to that, those early morning hours when you saw the tanks, had you ever seen any green berets or Croatian troops in the city?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Had you ever heard of green berets or Croatian troops taking over the town?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you able to go to and from work freely prior to that day?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever return to your job at the Mebos company after the conflict began?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: On the second day, when there was no more shooting, the fire died down, I went to my company. I stayed a few hours and I was told that, due to security reasons, we should return to our respective homes. The day after that, I also went to the companies, but the custodian at the gate of the company said that there would be no activity in the company as long as the situation was not stablised, and that we should stay at home up until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: During those two days that you went to your company, the Mebos company, how did you get there? By vehicle? On foot? By bicycle? How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I walked it, as I did in the past, but on this occasion, I saw many soldiers, known people, unknown people. I saw a big rally of people in front of the Cafe AS. They seemed to be enjoying themselves, happy. They were all in military uniform. They were all -- had arms. They had weapons there on the street, all those people that I had been seeing also before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you know a man at the time by the name of Jusuf Subasic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: He was a colleague of mine from -- he worked in the same company. And two days after, he came to me, to my courtyard, and he told me, "From today onwards, I'm the one who will be informing you about your labour assignments. You and your sons should report -- should report tomorrow morning at 6.30." And that is what I was doing, and he was informing me up until the day that I was imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, prior to starting the labour, did you have to go to the TO, Territorial Defence building?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, he told me to report to the Territorial Defence headquarters vis-a-vis the police station. There was quite a number of people, quite a number of Muslims and Catholics. We were entering one by one, a column. A young person was sitting at the table. I didn't know him. He took our names, surnames, and we then had to sign. After that, we left. But next to him was also standing another person in uniform. Everybody was in uniform except us who were standing in line. We were also told that we were to wear white armbands, all the Muslims and Catholics who signed up, and that we wear these all the time. When I returned home, the same Subasic Jusuf came and informed us that the next day, my son should report, and myself, in front of the factory Buducnost, and to report to -- It was in the same street, Edvarda Kardelja, next to my company. He didn't tell us why we should come and report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Weiner. I wonder whether line 13 of page 22, factory Buducnost and report to -- and we have a blank. Could you ask the witness to give the name again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the courier told you that you had to go to the Buducnost company and report to -- was there a certain individual you had to report to?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The courier came to my garden, that we report in front of the company Buducnost the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. He didn't tell you that you had to report to a certain person at that company?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let us go back to the visit to the TO building. Who went to the TO? Did you go with your son on that date?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you had to register your name or put your name on a list of some kind, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I signed -- I signed next to where my name and surname were typed. That was I, myself, and then my son.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And people of what ethnic group had to register?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Only Muslims and Catholics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you see any Serbs registering?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And they told you that you had to wear an armband, a white armband of some kind?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how did you feel about having to wear a white armband?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I felt the same as Jews must have felt during the Second World War, and I looked at my son and realised he was feeling the same way. We both were very sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And people of what ethnic group had to wear the white armbands?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Only Muslims and Catholics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, the next day, did you report to the Buducnost factory?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: My son and I reported that day, wearing white armbands. We were standing in the yard of the Buducnost factory and the entire group consisted of Muslims and Catholics only. Do you want me to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sure. And these Muslims and Catholics that were at the Buducnost factory, were they wearing white armbands?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: All of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, were there any Serbs there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: There were Serbs, including Simo Zaric, but they were standing next to the building. There were five or six of them standing right next to the building of the Buducnost factory, but not with our group. And then, a truck passed by and came to a halt. A young man came out of the truck. I didn't know him. And he cursed our mothers, and he told us "I'll show you all," using a swear word. "Let Igor Rukavina come out." This man, Igor Rukavina, was standing perhaps a few steps away from me. He was wearing an armband, a white armband, the same as I. This man grabbed him by the arm and took him away. And those commanders of theirs, Simo Zaric and the others, were standing nearby and watching, but nobody did anything about it. I covered my eyes with my hand and didn't see how it ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Another man came out whom I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Please continue. Tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Later on, a man came out by the name Jovica. I knew him. He was standing next to the Lukic house. I didn't hear what he was saying. I just looked at my child and thought "Is it possible that something like this is happening in our times?" I looked at the faces of the others, and I thought they didn't know either what was going to become of them, just as those Jews. I'm really speechless. I have no words to describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This Jovica, did he address the crowd?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: He addressed this group. He started making a speech, but I really couldn't bear to listen. He was saying something like everything was going to be all right, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that there was a group of Muslims and Croatians standing in one group, and there was a group of Serbs. Where were they in relation to the group of Muslims and Croatians?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: In front of us. Six men were standing in front of us, including Simo Zaric, who was wearing a military uniform. He wasn't saying anything. He was just standing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were they facing you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, after Jovica finishing speaking -- how long did he speak? For how long, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: All of it lasted for no more than an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What happened after it finished?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: We went our separate ways. We went home. One group went to perform labour, including my son. They were to dig bunkers in the direction of the Bosna River. My son came back home late. That same day, a young man by the name of Nurkic got killed. His year of birth was 1977. He was the son of Galib Nurkic. He was killed while digging bunkers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was he one of the labourers that were digging bunkers or trenches with your son?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: He was digging right next to my son. He was digging bunkers, bunkers were the first thing that had to be built at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I wonder if you could find out from the witness what was the age of his son at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us the age of your son, sir, at that time? What was your son's date of birth?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: My son was born on the 8th of March, 1971. At the time, he was studying at the machine engineering faculty in Sarajevo, in the second year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you go home. What happens next? Do you see Jusuf Subasic next with your assignment, or do you know when to report? What happens?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Subasic, Jusuf Subasic, came and told us that the next day at 6.00, we should report at the yard of the home for the elderly, the pensioners' home, for a labour action which eventually lasted until the 24th of December without a break. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When he told you to report, was that a request, or was that an order?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It was an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The next day, what did you and your son do?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: We reported outside the pensioners' home at 6.00, and we were waiting to be given a schedule, an assignment, where we were supposed to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were there any other people there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: There were many of us, over a hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were these only men, or were there women, too?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Men and women.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Of what ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Muslims and Catholics only.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were they wearing anything on their arms?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: We were all wearing white armbands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So what happens? There's a whole group of you out there.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: We were waiting to be given our work assignments. My first assignment on the first day was to go to Grebnica and dig bunkers. Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sure. Tell us about -- how did you get there, first, to Grebnica?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: They loaded us into a truck and drove us to the Tovirac village, perhaps a kilometre away from the first front line. And then we walked straight to the front line and we did our digging at the front line. I dug bunkers at first, and then I covered them. They brought wooden platforms for rails and we used them to cover the bunkers. And I emphasise, this was right at the front line. And then later, I covered the bunker with earth and camouflaged it with grass and shrubs so it cannot be distinguished from the background from a distance. It was the front line. You could expect a bullet to hit you at any moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, let's talk about this front line. Could you see soldiers while you were out there digging?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The soldiers were standing right next to us, and they were watching. A soldier was watching me until I finished my work. He was lying down on the ground so that he could not be seen. When one bunker was finished, when I and my group finished digging, because we didn't dig alone, there were 10 or 15 of us, then the soldier would get into it. But they were very insolent soldiers who actually shot at us while we were digging, because I was standing above them. They were shooting at us, and we begged them not to do that. And we could also be seen from the other side, because we were above. We were standing higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to object to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says, "There were solders shooting on us." This is not exactly what the witness stated. It says they were shooting but not on them. So it is my understanding that in this transcript it seems that soldiers were shooting on people who performed working assignments. So if my colleague could clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think the Prosecution will clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, while you were working, you said that there were soldiers near you. Let's just take it one step at a time. Of what ethnic group with these soldiers who were near you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: All of the soldiers were members of the 4th Detachment. All -- and I knew them all. In terms of ethnicity, they were Serbs and a couple of Muslims who had joined the detachment. I knew them all personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, while you were digging -- all right, actually, let me take a step back from that. Were there soldiers facing them on the other side? Was there another army facing the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you see those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: We couldn't see them, but we could see from which direction shooting was coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell us about the shooting. Was there shooting going on while you were out there digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I wonder whether we could clarify page 29, lines 2 and 3: "We couldn't see them, but we could see from which direction shooting was coming." Could we know who -- what ethnic background the "them" are and from which direction the shooting was coming?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You heard the Judge's question. You've got the 4th Detachment over here. You are down in front of them digging trenches. Who was on the other side?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: On the other side, facing them, that's Grebnica village, were Catholics, people defending their villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say "Catholics," you mean --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: And that was the HVO army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You mean the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No, not the Croatian army, but the troops of those local Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. So are you -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: One intervention. The witness said in line 21, "after the local war," he added "HVO," which means "Croatian Defence council," and it was not in transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner, please clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We just need a clarification for the transcript. Sorry about that. The troops that were involved in the shooting on the Grebnica side, was that local Croatian troops or local Croatian troops plus HVO?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Those were local soldiers, people defending their own homes, but they had a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what was the name of those local soldiers or the group that they were from, these Bosnian Croatians?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I learned about it later. It was the HVO, the Croatian defence council, but I found out about that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, there are two armies, and you're out there digging trenches. Where are you located in relation to the two armies?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I was straight at the trenches of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And as you are digging, you are standing. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And are there any barriers or any sort of equipment to protect you from shooting?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: There was nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And was there shooting going on?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The people for whom I was digging trenches were shooting across at the other trenches. And shooting was coming from the other side as well, so at any moment, any of us could have been killed. I will tell you later, if you ask me, about a man who was wounded while he was standing right next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- we'll get to that. Now, so you're standing between the firing. How did you feel at that time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: How can a man feel if he can get killed at any moment? It was certainly unpleasant, and it was also very hard manual labour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour. I would like one clarification. The witness kept saying that he was actually digging the trenches on the spot where the 4th Detachment was placed. And my learned colleague is insisting that the witness has been between the two firing sides. Whether we can really clarify this, because as my learned colleague has put it, and it's in the transcript right now in 31.3, it appears that the trenches were dug and there was a shooting from behind their back and shooting from the other side as well. I would just ask for a clarification, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sure, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Occasionally, we were digging trenches exactly at the place where the soldiers were standing, but I also went in front, outside the trenches, to make a clearing so they can see better, to cut grass. When I went forward in front of the trenches, I was actually standing between the two sides on all the three locations where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many people were with you digging those trenches?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: There were 10 or 15 men at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Of what ethnic group were the people that were digging the trenches?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: They were 90 per cent Muslim, and a couple of Catholics who hadn't been locked up yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were there any Serbs out there digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were the people who were digging trenches wearing armbands?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: We were all wearing armbands from the moment when we gathered outside the Buducnost factory until the end, and we had to wear them all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say "we," what ethnic groups had to wear the armbands?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Muslims and Catholics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, what hours did you work on that first day? What hours were you out there digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: From 6.00, when we would report, they would take us out at 7.00 or 8.00 in the morning, and then we worked until 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And during those 11 to 12 hours that you were there, did they feed you any meals?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Two slices of bread and a piece of something from a tin can in between, and the ration was the same on all days when I did the digging. There was nothing more than that. I don't think the soldiers fared much better in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was that a sufficient meal for you, for the workers?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, was there anyone guarding you prisoners? I shouldn't say "prisoners." Was there anyone guarding you workers?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Whenever I went out to work, we were always accompanied by Mila Pancir. He was the one guarding us always. He had some sort of old sniper rifle, and he would always stand by and tell us stories and brag that he had killed a couple of people. But he was always the one who took us out to do the digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: On the first day, was your son with you while you were digging on those front lines?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: My son was not together with me. He had a different assignment, digging at Brvnik. That is a different location on the same line, also the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, let's go to the next day. Did you go to the retirement home in the morning?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what happens on that next day?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: All the days were the same then. We would always report, wait to be given a work assignment, get on to a truck, and go to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what time did you get to the retirement home the next day?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where were you assigned? Where did they send you on that date?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The first ten days, my job was to dig those trenches at Grebnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how did you get there during those next nine days?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Always the same way. They would drive us to Tovirac village, and from there on we would walk to the front line. We would dig again, also trenches, but a bit further away. Some people were digging bunkers, and other people yet were digging connecting trenches leading to those bunkers. When we were -- when we ran out of rails, we cut trees. We felled trees, and we covered the bunkers with that. But the job was the same essentially.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you explain that. What do you mean, "when we ran out of rails"? What did you do with rails and what type of rails are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: We are actually talking about the wooden planks on which you set rails when you are building a railroad. We ran out of those, so we started cutting trees. And we put those trees on top of the bunker. Our job was to cut a tree, carry it on your shoulders to the bunker, lay it on top, cover it with earth, and the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you like to break there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we shall take our break for half an hour and continue the proceedings at 16.15 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner, the Prosecution continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, as we left off, you were out digging bunkers on the front lines for the next nine days. You worked there the first day, and then for the next nine days. And during those nine days, what hours were you out there digging bunkers?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was just the same from the first day. At 6.00 in the morning, I go to the retirement home. Then we go by truck. We go to the location at Tovirac village, and the same type of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What time would you finish?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately at 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what time would you get home?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I needed about an hour to come home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And on those -- on each of those ten days, how many meals did you receive a day during that 13-hour period?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It was the same meal, the same type of meal, and it was one meal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And once again, please describe what that meal was.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Two pieces of bread, and inside, some tin food product. It was pate, tinned pate, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they give you any coffee breaks during the day?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when the shooting broke out, then we all had to go and withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during these ten days that you were working - you mentioned the first day - but during the next nine days, was there much gunfire while you worked?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: On these locations, when I was working at Grebnica and the other locations, there was always gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And from which side was the gunfire coming?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: From both sides, you know. These from where we were digging, they were shooting but also gunfire came also from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you have to work during the gunfire?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you said on occasion, you had some breaks when the shooting broke out. What sort of shooting was that? Was that artillery fire? Was that just basic gunfire? When did they stop you from working?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was both an artillery fire or also basic gunfire. And we had to find shelter, and all who were on the front line, they -- the shooting would break out. It wasn't heavy artillery fire, it was maybe tremblants. But this was happening in Grebnica. And in Tutensenavac [phoen], it was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said it wasn't heavy gunfire. It was maybe something. The transcript didn't pick up what you indicated. Was there another type of artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: When I was digging, yes. When I was digging in Jeskovac [phoen], in Brvnik. In Jeskovac, there was a tank which was located along the first front line. And there was a tank and a Praga tank. And this was real, real artillery fire with grenades falling and shelling all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That was later at those other locations, not during the first ten days. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when the gunfire was occurring, where were you standing?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Usually, mostly I was above the trench or above the bunker.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you describe this as dangerous work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was it hard work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How did you feel at the end of the day?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I was very tired and miserable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Why were you miserable?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was thinking of my child. I was always thinking of my children. There was my child who was also doing the same work. You know, I wasn't thinking so much of myself, but the fact was I could have been killed any moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, during that first ten days, was anyone that was working with you injured?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: During the first ten days, I mentioned that Nurkic that was close to River Bosna. But in these locations where we were, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When Galib Nurkic was killed while digging trenches on the front line, that was while digging trenches with your son?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, along the banks of Bosna River. I've mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicated that Mile, whose nickname was Pancir, was with you during the digging?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Always.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And was he some sort of supervisor or guard, or what was his position?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he would supervise, and he would also issue orders what to do, where we were to dig. You were supposed to dig such and such, trenches or a bunker should be dug out here and here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was he in uniform?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Always.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you said he was armed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: He was always armed. He had a sniper rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you know a man by the name of Stojan Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: A colleague who worked with me on the same machine in the company Mebos.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him during the war, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: He was nonstop in front of the building of the retired people, and he always needed somebody who would work for him. He was in uniform, always armed like Mile, except that he had a Kalishnikov -- and he always needed workers, either for looting or other needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was he also a supervisor of the labourers?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you told us that you worked from a short time after the conflict, so we'll say in April of 1992, through December of 1992. Could you tell us by category, if we could do this, what type of work you performed, what type of work that you were ordered to perform?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Except for digging trenches, I also worked on many other jobs. But all these other jobs related to looting. I visited Tramosnica, Vranica, Dubica, Srpska Tisina, Hrvatska Tisina, Novo Selo. I worked there and I performed various jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's try and discuss some of these jobs. You mentioned you dug trenches at Grebnica, and then you also mentioned that you dug trenches at Lijeskovica and Brvnik. Could you tell us what you did at those places, Lijeskovica and Brvnik?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: In Lijeskovica, I also dug trenches. Then I had to mow grass around the trenches. That was an important and dangerous front line. And then we would make covers for the bunkers. But soldiers were not from Samac. But they weren't in the same command. These were soldiers from Krajina. I would dig for them trenches, but I had to go in front of the bunkers -- trenches. The trenches were low. And I had to mow, mow, and remove the grass. And in Grasnica, you had a dike. So we also had trenches and bunkers between buildings. There was a tank behind one building, and then after another one, a Praga cannon, or something similar, a similar type of arm. It was much more difficult than in Grebnica. It was more difficult for digging, for work. So we were brought in. We were brought in again by Mile. He shows us what we would Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. do, where to dig. But here, it was more dangerous for our lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was there shooting while you were out there digging and building these bunkers?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was shooting going on nonstop. It was real shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "real shooting"?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Here, there was nonstop exchange of fire from both sides, and we had mortar fire, then rifle exchange of fire. There was too much ammunition, too many arms, or maybe it was done out of fear. And the front line was -- were quite close here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how many days did you spend at these other locations, locations other than Grebnica, digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Most of the period of this forced labour, I spent in digging trenches, in digging, be it in the first, second, or third location.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But how long did you spend? Did you spend a few days, a few weeks, a few months? How long a period did you spend doing this?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I worked five days, then I had a break of a month, and then I'd be returned to the same location. That's -- it wasn't that I worked in continuity. After Grebnica, then I would go immediately to other locations. There would be a break, and then I would go back to Grebnica. I didn't know exactly where I would be sent up until the moment they told me where to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: The persons who did this work, this trench digging during the gunfire, of what ethnic group were they?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Catholics were -- 90 per cent were arrested. And 90 per cent were Muslims. So maybe there was equal. Maybe two or three Croats in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were there any Serbs out there working, digging these trenches, making these bunkers?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Never, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many men would be on one of these assignments working with you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Always between 10 and 15. Between 10 and 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was anyone ever injured from this gunfire in Lijeskovica or Brvnik?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Some 2 metres from me, maybe a bit more, Bobic was wounded, Bobic, the son of Salem. And he was injured -- wounded in the thigh. He was a bit bent, and he was wounded. They came with the car to pick him up. And I met him a few years later. He told me that they took him to the hospital in Brcko and after that he was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you volunteer for this work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you want to do this work, this digging of trenches?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did anyone that you know of volunteer for this work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did anyone want to do it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How did you feel about doing this work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was hard, physical labour, and I felt miserable. I felt humiliated. One cannot feel well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever do any type of agriculture or farming-type work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was sent to work in the field kitchen for Serbian soldiers in Serbian Tisina. There was seven of us. And we received an assignment from one of the soldiers, one of the foremen. He took us to the Catholic Hrvatska Tisina village. Then there was no Catholics there any more, cleansed. We were asked to harvest potatoes, tomatoes, whatever was needed for the field kitchen for their soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you do that harvesting, picking of vegetables, fruit, in the fields?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what we were doing: picking the vegetables, tomatoes, potatoes, onions, whatever was needed in order to prepare meals, to cook food, from that -- the gardens surrounding the houses and also from the fields. Wherever they found the locations where there were these produce, they told us to go and we would pick it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you said you did this in Hrvatska Tisina. Is that within the municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you did this, when you went to these locations to pick, was there a supervisor or a guard, or was there someone with you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do you recall who was with you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Todorovic, that was the surname. But it's the first building on the left near the bridge when you move through Korpara. I know when we would pick these vegetables, we were also asked to loot certain houses for certain objects. And we would take that to him. I didn't know this man before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's take a step back. When you started this work, this farming-type work, did you begin your day in Bosanski Samac at the retirement home?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
