utterances.text: Where did you begin your day?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: From my home, I went in the same direction. I passed the home of Mustafa Smajic. Then I crossed the railroad station, and we had to appear at the same -- in the same location.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did someone tell you to go to that location?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I was told that on the first day, when I was told to go and work there, that -- I was told that in front of the pensioners' building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you went to Hrvatska Tisina after you were told to go there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you said you thought it was a Catholic village. Why do you say you believed it to be a Catholic village?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Because I knew quite a number of people from that village. It was a Croatian -- these were Croatians. But at that point, there wasn't a single inhabitant living there any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What happened to the inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Some fled, and some died.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What was the condition of the housing in the village when you got there, as much as you could see?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: All the houses looked pretty miserable, pretty run down. In front of one, a house, I saw at the threshold a dog, and I felt miserable wondering whether his owner would ever return or not. A village which existed and doesn't exist any more, without a single inhabitant, without anything. I did see many Serbian soldiers and civilians from Srpska Tisina who entered these buildings and who would take out whatever they could. And so did we. We went in with the supervisor, who told us what to take out, a couch. But he preferred farming. I had to take out the pipes, irrigation pipes, out of one of the fields for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And who was that supervisor that you took the pipes out for?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That was the one Tovorac [Real-time transcript read in error "Todorovic"] in the first building after the bridge on the left in Srpska Tisina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's continue on the farming and agricultural --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I believe the witness has said that was the one Tovorac, I believe, not Todorovic. If my colleague can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the name. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you testified you said the name Tovorac. And in the transcript, it says Todorovic. What was the name of the supervisor who had you remove those pipes so we can clarify this record?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: In Tisina, there was no Todorovic. This was just a slip of the tongue. Tovorac. I'm not even sure of that, but I know where he is and where he lives. I could show you the house. Prior to that, he worked -- he worked in Samac. The first building on the left when going from Samac, first his brother's home in Srpska Tisina, and then his home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's continue on with the agricultural-type work. Did you ever work in the silos in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where were these silos located?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: At the exit from the town towards Srpska Tisina, near the railroad track and the railroad station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court, what did you do in the silos?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there I had to work, and I -- we were peeling corn cobs and we had this machine which we were turning. We were a pair working on that. And then we were also loading bags on trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how long did you do that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this job lasted some five or six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what were the conditions in the silos?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Very dusty, hard work, and the machine for husking had to be turned by hand, if you can imagine. Those who were there know what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you were removing the corn from the cob itself, the pieces of corn from the cob?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you place it by hand in a manual machine, mill. You then have -- you place a number of cobs and then you have to turn the machine, the handle. And I've never done that in my life up until then but that's what I did at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever work with any type of cattle?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I did two types of jobs involving cattle. For only two days, I worked at the Zasjeka on maintenance, and I also had the job of catching runaway cattle and pigs. And we would load them on to trucks, those pigs that we found at large in the fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And in what town or village did you do this work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: At first, there were only a couple of villages, one of them being Hrvatska Tisina, and later in Tramosnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, were there any lists ever made of the crops that you seized, that you picked from local farms, or the animals that you seized?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was any receipt or notice left at any of those residences or farms as to what was taken?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you trained for any of this agricultural work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you volunteer for this work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you want to do this work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The farms that were looted or that had crops taken and animals seized, of what ethnic group did these farms belong to?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: They all belonged to Catholics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever -- let's move on to another area of work. Did you ever collect wood or chop wood or chop trees for firewood or do anything related to wood or coal?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And tell the Chamber in what villages did you do that work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That was in town. I did most of that job in Odzak. In Odzak we would go from house to house with a small TAM truck, and first we loaded already-chopped wood for the purposes of shops in Samac and also to meet the needs of civilians of Serb ethnicity. I, for instance, delivered wood to two women in Samac. We would put the chopped wood into sacks, load the sacks, and deliver them. And in the houses of those two women, I had to take them up to the balconies. Those -- that was small chopped wood that fitted right in the fireplace. And then we loaded also bigger chunks of wood we delivered to Serb families. We unloaded them outside their houses. We couldn't carry a lot, because it was a small TAM truck. There were two of us. The other man was a former schoolmate of mine, Mersad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, the wood that you got, you said you got it from homes. From the homes of persons what ethnic group did you seize this wood?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The homes were 90 per cent Muslim homes in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what about the -- did you go to any Croat homes to seize --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you seize wood from any Serb homes?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you said you transported this back to Bosanski Samac. How did you know what homes to bring this wood to?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The driver would get his assignment or an order. The driver who drove us always knew to which house he had to take us, and he would tell us where to unload.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did the driver have a written list, or was it just a verbal order that he received?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: He knew. He had a list of houses where we were to unload, and we would do that. It depended on the wishes of the owner whether we would unload it outside the home or take it inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where did the driver get the list or the orders of persons who wanted wood? From whom did he get this list?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: On all occasions when I did this job, the driver would get a piece of paper from Dzevad Celic outside the retirement home. It was a list of people who were to go with Dzevad Celic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where did Dzevad Celic get the information?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Dzevad Celic got his information from Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who was Dzevad Celic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, he used to be my manager, the director. And later, he assumed that position, whether voluntarily or as work duty, I don't know. He just got that assignment and executed the orders which came from Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say he got the assignment, what did he do? What was his assignment in relation to the labour?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: He only decided on the number of people who were to go and do a certain job. He didn't have any powers to make any decisions himself or decide on jobs that would be done. He would just decide which people were to go and perform a certain job.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who made those decisions? If Dzevad Celic didn't make those decisions, who made the decisions of which people were to go and perform a certain job?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it depended on what the Serbs needed for their homes or businesses. He got his orders from upstairs, so to speak, from the office of Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And who did Dzevad Celic work for?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: He worked for Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How do you know, sir, that Tadic gave Dzevad Celic -- that Miroslav Tadic gave Dzevad Celic lists or orders as to who get firewood for? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: There was no other person except for him who made such decisions. Dzevad Celic told me that. And other people to whom I delivered wood told me the same thing. They would go to see Tadic, and then they would be referred to Celic, get a certain number of people who would then go to work for them. And that's how I went out to work several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's just talk about the firewood. Did you ever talk to any of the people who you got firewood for who they went to see to order this firewood and the labour to get the firewood? Did you talk to any of these people?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I talked to them, but actually it was more a case of them talking to me of their own accord. They told me that they had been to see Miro Tadic. They would get from him a piece of paper, and then they would go to Celic and get a certain number of people, workers. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever speak to the drivers of the trucks that you transported this wood about who gave the orders relating to the firewood?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what did the drivers tell you about who was giving the orders about who was to get firewood? What did they tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So they told you Tadic was giving the orders, Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, once they knew who to get the wood for, you would drive to houses in Odzak and elsewhere. How did you know which house to stop at? Did you stop at every house, or how did you know where to go? What would happen?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The driver of the truck would stop by a house and told us to unload. I never knew in advance where it would be. He knew everything that he had to know, what type of wood, which house where we were to unload.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you got to these houses in Odzak and elsewhere, did they just send you in and tell you to look for wood, or what would they tell you? Would they tell you to look for coal, wood? What were your directions?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Go and enter this house or this yard, because they were afraid lest it had been mined. First, they told us to look for chopped wood. We would go in. If we didn't find anything, we would go on. When we would find it finally in another house, we would load the truck to capacity. For the needs of businesses, we would just heap it on the truck. And for the needs of private persons, such as those two women I had mentioned, we would first put the wood into sacks and load them on to the truck. They lived on the second floor above Merkur, and we delivered it all the way up to the second floor, and then we would go back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That was the two women that you got the wood for.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I knew those two women personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, the homes that you would take this wood from, of what ethnic group were these people?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Most of the people in Odzak who were Muslims and Catholics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you take wood from any homes owned by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you take items other than wood from those homes?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. The driver always needed something. Women were also with us. For instance, when we went to Trkic, we were always accompanied by women who needed a couch or an armchair or anything nice we found in a house that hadn't already been taken away, we would pick up. And that was in addition to our regular job that we did always. Every time we went out, we had to take out something and carry it away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that the drivers did not accompany you into these houses because they were scared that they were mined. Could you explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Everybody was afraid. It might be the case, but nobody was actually ever injured. But just in case, we were always the first to go into a house, we, the workers, and they followed. And then they would point their finger and say, "Pick this, this, and that, and take it away." But nothing ever happened in terms of mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The workers that you were talking about, the people who went in first, or just the workers in general, of what ethnic group were they?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Muslims, and a couple of Catholics. As time went by, there were fewer and fewer Catholics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What was happening to the Catholics that there were "fewer and fewer Catholics"?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Tadic put them in camps and used them for exchanges because their village -- because their village on the other side was also occupied. He had his chance to use these people to set up an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The work that you were doing, collecting the firewood, bringing it places, transporting it, bringing it upstairs to homes, was it hard work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you want to do this type of work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The drivers that brought you to these places and told you to go into different buildings or homes, where were they from?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The drivers were people I knew. They were employed in Samac. They mostly came from the town of Samac and the surrounding villages. I knew them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Of what ethnic group were these people?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were they armed when they brought you to places?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: They all carried weapons. In fact, they had weapons, but they usually left them on the truck. They didn't carry it with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you brought this wood to homes, to homes or shops in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Bosanski Samac, of what ethnic group were the people who received this wood?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The homes belonged to people of Serb ethnicity. The shops, the businesses, belonged to companies from outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina, from Croatia. The shops which were not looted were from Belgrade, for instance, but there were not many of them. They didn't use much of his stuff. They had no use for it, simply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, the witness on page 51, lines 19 and 20, stated that Mr. Miroslav Tadic put the Catholics in camps and used them for exchanges. I wonder if you could clarify with the witness how he knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You've heard the Judge's question. Could you please explain?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Tadic is not originally from Bosanski Samac. He comes from the municipality of Odzak, the Novi Grad village. This Novi Grad was occupied by Catholics, and he put all Catholics in the building of the secondary school in detention, and later exchanged them. They were the first to get exchanged as a group. That's why he had detained them, in order to use them for an exchange to get his people from his native village. I know this for sure, and the Catholics from Bosanski Samac were the first to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The information that you have relating to these exchanges, where did you get that information? Did you talk to certain people? Did you see certain things that were happening? How did you obtain this information? What's the source of your information?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That camp was the first to be disbanded. It simply disappeared. All that remained were those few Catholics from the town of Samac who had been detained in the Territorial Defence buildings, together with the Muslims. That is something that happened, and I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to anyone who had been exchanged as part of this process?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I talked to a number of people, quite a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did they tell you about how they were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That exchange was with Croatia. All the exchanges were with Croatia. I, too, was later exchanged and went to Croatia. A lot of people asked to be exchanged, and the Croats wanted Croats first, which is logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, let us just finish up with the wood and then we'll get to exchanges a little bit later, sir. Did you ever cut trees? Were you ever ordered to cut trees?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Branica, which is a hamlet of Obudovac village. I spent ten -- or up to ten days there. There, we cut trees for fighting men who had been killed. In fact, for their families, mothers, wives, whoever had a family member who had been killed. We cut those trees, loaded them on to a tractor, and drove them away. Those were not big logs. Those were more like planks, about three metres in length. We would pile them on to a tractor and drive them to the house in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was this hard work, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It's very hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you want to do this work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you volunteer for this?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know anyone who volunteered for this type of work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many people did this with you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: There were ten of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Of what ethnic group were these people?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And was wood ever brought, this wood or any other wood, or coal ever brought to any Muslim or Croat homes?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Those logs, in fact, this wood was transported to Obudovac village, to Serb Homes. Nobody else lives there actually. There were only Serbs there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about the wood that was brought to Bosanski Samac? Was that ever brought to Muslim or Croat homes?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you involved in collecting and transporting construction goods and materials? Did you ever do that? Were you ever assigned to do that or ordered to do that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What type of materials did you collect and load?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Construction materials. Bricks, they are called "block bricks." Planks. Wire. We would stop at yards, and wherever we found stuff they were interested in, we had to carry it away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In what areas or villages or municipalities did you take these materials?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: For two days running, I went to Tramosnica village. It is in Gradska municipality, not in Samac. On the first day, we brought back a large truck full of block bricks, and we unloaded them at Samac Trans company. I did the same job the next day. We went to Tramosnica, loaded the bricks. But this time around, we unloaded them at Zasjeka. And then it turned out a mistake had been made, so we put them back on the truck and drove them to Samac Trans.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you go to any other villages in the municipality of Bosanski Samac to do this work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: This type of work which we carried out in Bosanski Samac, we went to Hrvatska Tisina, a similar job. We worked in the same way. Whatever we found, we loaded trucks. And then I unloaded also wooden planks in the railroad station in Bosanski Samac Agropromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say Agropromet, you mean the Agropromet warehouse near the railway station?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes. And that warehouse, I unloaded from a truck, planks. With my son, we unloaded -- it was cement, cement also in bags, in sacks. I was always -- I had the luck of unloading always the same type of truck, the same truck which was driven by somebody from Kruskovo Polje. I knew them personally. Then Subasic would come, and we would go -- in addition to my daily work, we would go in the evening and unload this truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, the homes that you took and businesses that you took these materials from, the wood, the planks, wire, cement, of what ethnic group were the people who owned these homes?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I didn't understand. From where we took?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. The homes that you got all of these materials, these construction materials from, of what ethnic group were the people who owned those homes?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You were seizing the construction materials from the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. People of what ethnic group lost their materials or had these materials stolen from them?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, these were Catholics. And Odzak was a Muslim -- with a Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever seize materials, these construction materials, from the homes or businesses of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And all of these materials were eventually brought back and stored in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever go to stores and take food or groceries?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I participated directly in one looting. It was Cviko Tesic and Torak [phoen] who went. That was an abandoned store owned by a person whose nickname was Romeo. His home was near the Catholic graveyard. We collected everything, placed it on the truck and then drove to Agropromet where the warehouse was near the police station. That was -- then I remained in there. Somebody who knew me, I would receive that, those goods, and then I would place it on the shelves in the warehouse. So that was also a job that I performed for a number of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did anyone else take food and groceries from shops in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: All the shops were looted immediately a month later. At that point then certain commissions came out and sealed off these premises, all the shops which were owned by Muslims or Catholics which were private, and shops which were not from Bosnia, which were from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about the shops which were owned by persons from Croatia? Were those looted, too?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: All of them. All of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about shops that were owned by Serbs? Were they looted?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No. They continued to operate normally. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about shops owned by companies from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody touched those shops.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, the shops that were looted, such as the Romeo store in Bosanski Samac, after it was looted, was any receipt left or any list of items taken left there to show what was seized?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Never. They -- when we would bring in the Agropromet warehouse, the goods then, Sejkto Pasic [phoen] and Pero Travorac [phoen] would make a list of inventory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, these two men you just named that would make an inventory, who did they work for?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: They worked for Mr. Miro. They had -- they were always close to him and to his office. I saw them there close three, four times. They were older people. In the past, they were shop salesmen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say "Mr. Miro," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do these two men that you were referring to have offices?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they -- next to Tadic's office, they had a long table there. Not only them, but also some others. Some were making lists of buildings, of houses, and so on. But they were always there on the floor where his office was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So we're talking at the retirement home?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you loaded a truck with food and items, would that be from several stores or just one store, or would that vary?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I would load -- I directly unloaded -- I loaded from that one shop. But otherwise, I was unloading and placing it in the warehouse, piling. And wherever I would be told to put this, pile it up, I would. It wasn't only me; there were others who were doing this also.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is when an inventory was made back at the warehouse, would anyone ever ask where each of these particular items ever came from?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, were restaurants in Bosanski Samac ever looted?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: All of them. All of them that belonged to Muslims or Catholics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about the restaurants owned by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. They operated as they did in the past, including the AS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You mean Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, who was looting these restaurants in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the military -- the members of the 4th Detachment. They would -- this wasn't under any anybody's control. They would take what they needed, and also others coming from aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did anyone stop these members from the 4th Detachment from looting restaurants in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What time period was this?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately, at the beginning. That was the first. These were the first facilities to be looted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say "at the beginning," do you mean right after the conflict began in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with a company known as the Korpara company?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Korpara, yes, yes. I was loading. These were a factory producing wicker furniture, so I was working for the kitchen in Srpska Tisina. A person by the name of Mica, who doesn't see on one eye, we went with him. We filled up and loaded one truck. I don't know where he took it. Two or three hours later, he came. We reloaded the furniture from that factory hall. After that, I went back to the village of Tisina and resumed my work. So it was from this plant that we took it. There was nobody in that plant, in that factory, except for Mica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did someone supervise the work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this person by the name of Mica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what happened to the goods, the furniture that was loaded on to trucks from that factory?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All of this loading work, whether it was food or construction materials, was it easy work to do?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was loading food. It wasn't difficult. But as well as for the wicker furniture, it wasn't difficulty, but it took quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about the construction materials, was that difficult work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is difficult work. It's physical work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you volunteer for any of this work, any of the loading work, whether it was food or construction materials or the furniture?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you want to do this work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your occupation was as a machinist or a miller, milling machine specialist?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And this work had nothing to do with your occupation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you involved, sir, with the looting of homes?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was that part of your labour assignments?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In what areas were you assigned to loot homes?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: In Hrvatska Tisina, Novo Selo, Grebnica, Odzak, Hrvatska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever loot in Tramosnica?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. On two occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's start with Tramosnica. On those days you were going to loot -- actually, first, tell us, where is Tramosnica?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It is in the municipality of Gradacac. It is close to Pelagic, Slatine, and Gradacac. Somewhere in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with the village of Tramosnica? Had you been there prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I just passed through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you know anyone from the village?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I knew Kata, who -- Mensur's wife, who worked in Bosanski Samac. She had a law degree. And she was from Tramosnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know who type of village it was, of what ethnic group the people there came from?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Completely Catholic village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, on those days that you were sent to loot homes in Tramosnica, where did you gather in the mornings?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: We gathered in front of the home of the retired people. That is, there was this one time when I was to load buildings blocks, and then I went to Tramosnica when I was in Branica, the hamlet of Obudovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. You went to Tramosnica. How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: On a truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Once you got there, what did you do on that first day, the first of the two days in Tramosnica?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: We were loading building -- construction bricks, but I've already narrated that. We loaded the first day, the second day, and then we came back. And in Obudovac when we were felling trees for the dead soldiers' families, along the way we also loaded those little huts for the drying of tobacco leaves. I believe that I placed -- I moved two of these objects, and we took them to neighbouring villages, these platforms. And then I saw an American mobile home. It looked something like that. These platforms for drying tobacco.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about that. Did they grow tobacco in Tramosnica?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And was Tramosnica known for tobacco growing in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Our entire area was known for that, and in connection with that, also Tramosnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they have tobacco sheds in Tramosnica for drying tobacco?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what was the size of these tobacco sheds? If you can describe it in metres.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It's 2 and a half metres wide; and in length, some 4 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do they have a roof?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you took some of these sheds. Where did you see these sheds first? Were they in yards in were they in driveways? Where were these sheds located?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: In their yards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, what did you do with these sheds? Did you bring them to someone after you took them?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: We only loaded them on our truck trailers, trailers from which were otherwise pulled horse cart. We placed them on these carts, and they were taken away. But we didn't unload them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How did you know which sheds to take? Did someone select them? Was there a list? How did you know which sheds to take?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a person came -- that there were sheds. We loaded about ten of them, and there were people who wanted these sheds, and we helped them, then, to load them. It's not that we helped, but we did load them. We were the ones who loaded them then, and we placed them on the cart. And next to these sheds, you had also oil reservoirs, oil tanks, but we didn't remove that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, the sheds that were taken, they belonged to persons of what ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Catholics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And they were given or selected by persons of what ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So people just came and picked out a shed, and you had to take it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were supposed to load them. And then the people would take them away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: While you were in Tramosnica, did you ever loot any private homes?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was along the way -- for the needs of the driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the truck drivers who directed the looting of what they wanted or needed, where were they from?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: This one, this one with which we loaded the bricks was from Samac. For these tobacco sheds, that was a driver from Obudovac, but I didn't know him, the one who was driving us to there and then taking us back was from Obudovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you took items from homes, whether it was the sheds, items from homes, construction materials, any type of items, was any receipt or inventory made?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And let us move on to Odzak, municipality of Odzak. Did you ever loot any homes, private homes, in the municipality of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That was later when the Serbian army entered Odzak some 15 days later. That was in the second round of looting, and it included also my son.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was that in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how many people were sent to Odzak to loot homes?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a number of groups. I went with two people, and then my son was with a bigger group, and then there were groups also composed of women. All the women on those locations went there and worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how did you get to Odzak? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I went by tractor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long did you --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: And with a TAM truck, a small TAM truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Odzak looting homes?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I always went there for one day. I would always go for one day and then return home at dusk. In Dubica, when I went to Dubica, then I stayed for a longer period, and that's also in the municipality of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Within the municipality of Odzak, how many days were you there looting homes? Was it months? Was it weeks?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Days. In the municipality of Odzak, a month. But Odzak itself, a day, a few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you got there, a truck would bring you to homes. Was there a list of homes to visit to take things from, or did they just stop at every home on the street? What did they do once you got there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: There was no list, but we went from house to house to see what could be collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you what to take first or did they first, say, go in and see what you could steal, or what were you told?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they told us what they wanted us to take out. Somebody needed a couch, somebody an armchair. Anything that was nice was taken away. Anything that was well-preserved, not worn out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber some of the things that you took while you were looting houses in the municipality of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I told you about the wood already. And in the Odzak municipality, I did the same thing I did in Hrvatska Tisina. I would take anything they wanted from a house, starting with windows, a complete set of furniture, couches, armchairs. In Odzak, I removed an entire roof together with Ibrahim Trkosevic, my partner. We removed an entire roof and installed it on another house. First we measured the house, the length, the width. We found the same-sized house in Hrvatska Dubica, and installed that roof. We would take first the beams and then the tiles and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, we don't need the details. It's sufficient to say the roof and materials were removed and taken to another house. We will take a 15-minutes break and resume our proceedings at 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you indicated that you took all sorts of things from apartments in Bosanski Samac -- I'm sorry, in Odzak. Let's go finally to Bosanski Samac and the surrounding villages. Were you ever sent to loot any homes in those areas?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who accompanied you during these looting trips to the Bosanski Samac -- in Bosanski Samac and the surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The people who wanted things out of various houses, and the drivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say "the people who wanted things," are we talking about civilians from the area of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could any civilian just go along with you, or did they need some sort of permission?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I would be ordered to go with such and such a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what was the process? How did you come about to be ordered to go with a certain civilian to get a certain item for them?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: My messenger would tell me to accompany such and such a person, and to carry the things he or she needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did the messenger make the decision whether or not the civilian should go along with you, or whether or not they should receive whatever item, whether it's furniture, electronics, plumbing, that they needed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who would make the decision?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The person who needed something would go and see Tadic. Tadic would refer them to Dzevad Celic. Celic would assign a certain number of people, and the messenger would tell me where to go and what to carry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, how do you know about this process, that it went from Tadic to Celic and eventually down to the drivers and the workers? How did you know about this process?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I was told by the messengers, by Celic, by the people who wanted things, and I would also see them going to one and the same place always to ask for as many people as they needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You said you were told by Celic. What did Celic tell you about this process?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That he was there only to determine what number of people would go and perform a certain job, and to identify those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who did he tell you made the decision of what civilians could go along and receive items?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: He told me that this decision was always made by Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you say "Tadic," do you mean Miroslav Tadic, the defendant in this case?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you talked about Jusuf Subasic sometimes, the courier. Did you ever discuss this process of civilians going out with you labourers in getting certain items? Did you ever discuss this process with him?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did he tell you who authorised the civilians to accompany them and get the items they wanted?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who did he tell you authorised the requests?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: He told me that he was there only to execute, and that Tadic was making all the decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, how often did you go out with civilians to get items for them?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Those were occasional jobs. We did them from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what sort of items did you take from homes for these civilians?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: For civilians, it was usually furniture, various electronic items, washing machines, radios, anything that was in working order, anything that was good.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And of what ethnic group were these civilians that you went out with?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you just go out once with these civilians, or did you go out several times with certain civilians?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: With Rado, who was nicknamed "specialist," I went several times. She was the mother of Mile Pancir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what did you get when you went out on those several times with her?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: She liked everything, starting with sofas, armchairs, television set, if anything was in working order. Everything that was good. If there was lingerie, underwear that was in closets that was clean or good, anything and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you bring these items to her home?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did her home look like when you brought her these goods?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Her house is on my street. Even before the war, she wasn't poor, although she was rather modest. But she got really wealthy during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever loot a store in Bosanski Samac where the goods were taken outside of Bosnia, a store or a factory?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I was involved in the loading of a truck with stuff from Hrana Produkt. It's a big refrigerated truck. And out of that company, we took out frozen meat, pickled food, tins, delicatessen, and we loaded that on to trucks with Belgrade licence plates. And my son worked there as well. On one occasion, I watched from one of the houses, the first houses on the left-hand side in the direction of Srpska Tisina. That house is very near Hrana Produkt company.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you see those trucks drive off?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, was that difficult work at Hrana Produkt?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was very cold inside when we entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was that kind of like a giant freezer warehouse, freezer storage warehouse?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you have the proper clothing for working there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when did this occur, this work? In what month, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It was in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Sir, the looting work that you performed, did you know the owners of any of the homes that were looted?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: When I was looting this one house in Hrvatska Tisina, I knew most of the people, but in particular, Marko Karalic, the craftsman who taught me my skills. He also worked in the Mebos factory for a while. He was a very good man, and I helped him for a couple of months to unload stuff from a house nearby the railway station. And I took out coal from this garage-type structure and loaded it on to a truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How did you feel about looting your mentor's home?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That was one of the harder moments in that period I spent in Samac. The man with whom I had spent 30 years in our former enterprise who had taught me everything I knew, a wonderful man who was expelled from his home and had to leave. He was a good craftsman, and he was left without anything. He was reduced to loading coal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you want to do this looting work, or were you forced to do it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I was forced to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you want to do any of these labour assignments that you were given?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you volunteer for any of these labour assignments?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know anyone who volunteered for any of these labour assignments?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you refuse?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't dare to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Because I had two children, a wife, and I could see three camps set up in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you afraid?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you just a few more questions about the work. You said that you would start each morning in front of the retirement home. When you and this large group of people lined up in the morning, how were you treated in those mornings over that seven-month period, almost eight-month period that you worked?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Men gathered there. There was also a cafe, but we couldn't go inside, we, the people who had labour assignments. Soldiers went in to the cafe. Some people would greet us; some would spit at us; sometimes someone would show us the three-finger salute, and we had to reciprocate. They would go in and have a drink, come out and repeat the three finger salute and we would have to return it. It was all a sorry sight. Very miserable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you talk about a three-finger salute, what is the three-finger salute?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That's the Serb salute, with three fingers, the soldierly salute. They all used it to greet each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can you show us it again. Show us the three-finger...

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So for the record, it's the thumb and two fingers closest to the thumb. And you would --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the record reflect the witness is demonstrating.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you would have to respond if someone gave you that with that same salute?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That was the left hand?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Does it make a difference if it's left hand or right hand, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I am left handed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see. So some saluted with their right hand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They all saluted with their right hands. And I am left handed, so that's why I showed it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, during the period that you worked from April through the end of December, were you ever sick or injured?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I was a sick man even before that. I had trouble with my spine. But once when I was working in Branica, and since I am not very dexterous with axes and stuff like that, a tree fell on my foot and almost cut off one of the toes. But until the wound healed by itself, I continued working.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you in pain after that injury?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many days were you in pain after that injury?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: At least ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you stop working, or did you take some time off on sick leave?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How come?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't dare to go and see a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, during these seven-plus months that you were working, were you paid for any of the work that you had performed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long did your son work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Until the 25th of August, when he escaped across a mine field to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: From April until August, was your son ever paid for the work that he performed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you have any other relatives that worked?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: My brother-in-law worked, but only occasionally. My half brother worked. Anybody who was able-bodied worked, anybody who wasn't too old for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was your brother-in-law or half-brother paid for their work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you don't know anyone who was paid for their work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that while you worked on the front lines, you were fed one meal over an 11, 12-hour period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before we move there, the witness used to be employed before the break-out of the war. Did your salary continue to be paid from your former employment before the war? During the period when you were taking part in all these projects that you have been describing, was your normal salary being paid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't quite understand. Do you mean from my company?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Only this one time, Stojan Blagojevic came to see me, brought a list and told me to sign it, and said that some arrears for 15 days would be paid to us, but that was the last I saw of Stojan, and I never saw the money, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When did Stojan Blagojevic come to you with a piece of paper? When was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That was in the month of May, and that happened outside the retirement home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated previously that while you were working -- while you were digging trenches, you received one meal a day, one meal during a 12-hour period. During all those other jobs that you were forced to do, were you fed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: When I was working in Srpska Tisina, when I worked in this Serb kitchen, I could get some food from them. And when I went on the looting trips, I never got anything except if some of those people there gave me something. But that was only occasional. When I worked in Odzak, or rather, the Odzak municipality where I spent 20 days working for one man in his house, he would feed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: During that seven-month period, how often were you fed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, once a day. But when I went on those looting jobs, I never got anything to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you were fed, was it a sufficient amount of food for you and the other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were people losing weight?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. My learned colleague said "other prisoners." We never understood that this witness was a prisoner at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner, I think the terminology is...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was it a sufficient amount of food, sir? When you were fed, was it a sufficient amount of food for you and the other workers?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you or any of the other workers lose weight during this work period?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Everybody except for me. I am the way I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you have always been very thin and lanky, as we would say?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, who was in charge of this compulsory labour programme that you worked for seven months?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where was his office, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: His office was on the first floor of the retirement home, the room directly -- straight in front of you when you're coming up the staircase.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have any conversation with Dzevad Celic concerning who was in charge of the forced-labour programme?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And who did he say was in charge?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Only Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did Celic ever call you to his office concerning a work assignment?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court about that.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: He was my manager, my director, and he summoned me once. That was on the 26th of August. He wanted to issue me with an order to go out to work on the so-called separation. And that is the building of concrete bunkers, or more precisely, the making of concrete blocks from which bunkers are made. That is one of the hardest forms of manual labour. I told him, "Look, Celic. You were my manager. You know that I was seen by the disability commission three times. You know that I was about to get a disability pension." And he answered: "You have to go and ask Miro if you want to be released." But I didn't dare do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did he show you anything when he told you he wanted you to go to the separation company to work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He showed me a paper with the decision that I, with my name and surname, have been -- that it was decided that I would go and work in the separation plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you complained, did he tell you who made the decisions relating to -- all the decisions relating to the work, the assignments?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: He told me that it was decided by Tadic, the next floor, and that he cannot do anything about it himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you who could change that plan? Who was the person Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. who could change that assignment?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: He told me -- repeated it a number of times that only Tadic could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you've talked many times about a Jusuf Subasic, the courier. Did you ever discuss with him the power or the authority of Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had. He also said the same thing as Celic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That Miro Brcko is the one -- Tadic, Miroslav is the one who decides about everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, were you ever assigned to work at night? After you had completed a day, were you ever assigned to work at night by Subasic, this courier?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, once I mentioned that I was unloading the planks at the railroad station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what hours did you do that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That was after I returned from the previous work. It was somewhere at 8.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you want to do that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you tell Subasic that you didn't want to do that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did Subasic tell you who authorised him or who authorised your labour that night?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't say anything on that occasion, just that I had to go there and do the unloading operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever speak to any of the truck drivers concerning the labour programme?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had. I knew these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did they ever tell you who was in charge of the assignments and the decisions and plans relating to the assignment of labour?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Always the same answer: Tadic, with whomever I spoke, the same answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that Dzevad Celic showed you this assignment sheet when he called you on that one occasion to his office.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever see a similar document to the one that Celic showed you relating to the assignment of personnel for labour?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, when my father died.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court what happened when your father-in-law died.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: When my father-in-law died, I went to the retirement home. I met a few people along the way, and I asked whether they knew what the procedure was, whom to ask. I met Celic, and he said, "Go up to Miro's, because you'll need a truck." I went to Tadic's office. I asked him. I told him my father-in-law died. I asked, "Can you give me the small truck?" And he said: "At this point in time, I don't have it at my disposal. At this point, I don't have a single free truck at my disposal."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, while you were in his office to see about the truck, did you see anything?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I did see the identical type of paper as Celic had shown me when he told me that I was to go to work in the separation plant. I didn't see the content, but it was the same type of paper, the same type of form.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where did you see this document which was similar to the one that Celic had showed you assigning you to a certain job? Where did you see this similar-type document?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: In front of him on the table. He was standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say "he," whose table and who was standing?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Miroslav Tadic was in the office there. And he was standing at the desk. I entered, and I made the request.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And then you saw the paper on Tadic's table, then, in his office?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, during your period of work, did you wear a white armband?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Always.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you indicated you were on occasion given one meal a day. Were you hungry at the end of the day?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you tired?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If you weren't paid, how did you feed your family, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: My relative, my brother-in-law, helped me a lot. And then Ratko Tuvakovic, he would come around and bring something. And we -- I had one or two sacks of flour. Well, we somehow lived. We made the ends meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were the members of your family hungry?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did anyone in your family lose weight?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: My wife lost 40 kilograms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, during this period that you had to work, did you see -- did you happen to see any of the defendants in Bosanski Samac as you were working in different jobs all over that municipality and in many others? Just yes or no, if you saw any of them.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's start off with Miroslav Tadic. How often would you see Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Three times a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where would you see him?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: In front of the retirement home, when he was entering the building going up to his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you see him at any other locations?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I saw him twice, a few times in front of the home of Mustafa Raga, and also in front of some other houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, during your period of compulsory labour, did Mr. Tadic's dress or appearance change in any way?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he seems to me here today as he used to be when sitting in front of the hotel in Bosanski Samac. But at the time, he wore a long white coat, and he had a long beard and round spectacles. We presented himself as a Vojvoda, as a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say "presented himself as a commander," what significance did this long beard, round glasses and long white coat, long trench coat, what significance was that to your opinion?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in my view, he was imitating Draza Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And who was Draza Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That was a Chetnik Vojvoda commander during the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how did -- was this General Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how did he dress?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I could see in our films, it was something like that, except that he was a bit taller, heftier. At least, he was portrayed as such in films.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you see the defendant Simo Zaric in Bosanski Samac during the period that you were forced to work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how often did you see him?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see him that often. If I look back, approximately ten times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where did you see him during those ten times?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: On two occasions, in front of his sister's, in front of the sister's house, in front of Raga's house when I went to work on the silos. I saw him in front of the building of the Australian citizen. That's where the military command was, and the military command from Mustafa Raga's house. So they would move the command from one building to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say the Australian citizen, was this an Australian who was living in Samac that moved out? Could you tell us what that's about?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That building was erected by an Australian subject who built the house in Bosanski Samac. They were expelled. It was a very big house, a beautiful house, with a big cellar and also -- also a good shelter. And that is where the staff headquarters were. And also, Mustafa Raga's house was a big stable house, and that is where they moved to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say the "staff," you mean the military staff?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Simo Zaric at the retirement or pensioners' home?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I did see him on a number of occasions, just when passing by. He was going up to see Miro.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you saw Simo Zaric, how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Always in military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was he armed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Always a pistol -- a service pistol. And I saw him also with a bag in front of the sister's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What kind of bag, when you say a bag?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a soldier's service bag, shoulder bag, officer's bag. It's made of leather which is worn over the shoulder. It is not very big. Leather.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you saw the defendant Simo Zaric, was he with anyone?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Was --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was he ever with anyone?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: He had his driver who would drive him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
